{{Short description|Philosophical theory}}
In [[Philosophy]], '''logical holism''' is the belief that the world operates in such a way that no part can be known without the whole being known first. 

'''Theoretical holism''' is a theory in [[philosophy of science]], that a theory of science can only be understood in its entirety, introduced by [[Pierre Duhem]]. Different total theories of science are understood by making them [[Commensurability (philosophy of science)|commensurable]] allowing statements in one theory to be converted to sentences in another.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Dreyfus|first=Hubert L.|date=1980|title=Holism and Hermeneutics|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20127455|journal=The Review of Metaphysics|volume=34|issue=1|pages=3–23|jstor=20127455|issn=0034-6632}}</ref>{{Rp|II}} [[Richard Rorty]] argued that when two theories are incompatible a process of [[hermeneutics]] is necessary.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|II}}

'''Practical holism''' is a concept in the work of [[Martin Heidegger]] than posits it not possible to produce a complete understanding of one's own experience of reality because your mode of existence is embedded in cultural practices, the constraints of the task that you are doing.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|III}} 

[[Bertrand Russell]] concluded that "[[Hegel]]'s [[Hegelian dialectic|dialectical]] logical holism should be dismissed in favour of the new logic of [[propositional analysis]]."<ref>Michael Baur (ed.), ''G. W. F. Hegel: Key Concepts'', Routledge, 2015, p. 193.</ref> and introduced a form of [[logical atomism]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Russell|first=Bertrand|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jNOLAgAAQBAJ|title=The Philosophy of Logical Atomism|date=2009-09-10|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-22318-2|language=en}}</ref> 

A unique kind of holism is found in [[Chinese philosophy]], especially in the writings of the [[Tiantai]] school of Buddhism, beginning with the works of [[Zhiyi]]. The Buddhist studies scholar and philosopher Brook Ziporyn terms it "Omnicentric holism".<ref>Ziporyn, Brook. (2000). ''Evil and/or/as the Good'', pp. 112-113. Leiden, The Netherlands: Harvard University Asia Center. <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.1163/9781684170340</nowiki></ref>
